key_terms.meaning: Small molecule that joins with many identical or similar molecules to form a polymer.
Large molecule made of many monomer units joined by covalent bonds.
The smallest part of a polymer chain that repeats along the backbone.
Number of repeat units in one polymer chain; symbol DP.
Polymer made from two or more different monomer types.
Arrangement of side groups along a chain of stereocentres.
All side groups on the same side of the polymer backbone.
Side groups alternate regularly from one side to the other.
Side groups arranged randomly along the chain.
Chain-growth polymerization in which monomers add to an active centre without losing small molecules.
Step-growth polymerization between bifunctional monomers, often releasing a small molecule such as water.
Transition metal compound plus alkyl aluminium that polymerises alkenes with stereochemical control.
Fraction of polymer chains packed into ordered regions.
Covalent bonds joining separate polymer chains into a network.
Total mass of a sample divided by total number of chains; symbol Mn.
Average in which larger chains count more; symbol Mw.
Polymer with a conjugated backbone that can conduct electricity after doping.
Material made of two or more distinct phases, a matrix and a reinforcement, kept separate.
Continuous phase in a composite that holds the reinforcement and transfers load.
Strong phase in a composite that carries most of the applied load.

takeaways: A polymer is a macromolecule named from its repeat unit, and its classification follows monomer type, chain structure and thermal behaviour.
Tacticity controls how regularly side groups sit along a stereocentre chain, so it controls packing and crystallinity.
Addition polymerization is chain growth from an initiator; condensation polymerization is step growth between bifunctional monomers.
Ziegler–Natta catalysts insert alkene monomers in a fixed orientation and can make isotactic polymers.
Branching, cross-linking and crystallinity change chain packing, and packing sets density, stiffness and softening point.
Each important polymer is best learned as monomer, repeat unit, mechanism and one use.
A polymer sample has a distribution of chain lengths, so Mn, Mw and PDI must be matched to the measurement method.
A conjugated backbone plus doping turns an insulating polymer into a conducting polymer.
A composite combines a matrix and a reinforcement so the pair gives higher specific modulus than either phase alone.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for definitions plus classification, a mechanism with initiator or catalyst, structure–property reasoning, molar-mass averages, doping, and a matrix/reinforcement example, often joined in one question.

bank.q: Define polymer, monomer, repeat unit and degree of polymerization. Classify polymers by origin, thermal behaviour and chain structure, with one example for each class.
outline: definitions with correct symbols and terms

bank.q: Explain tacticity in a vinyl polymer. Compare isotactic, syndiotactic and atactic chains and state the effect of each on crystallinity.
outline: three tacticity patterns described in words
isotactic and syndiotactic pack better than atactic

bank.q: Compare addition and condensation polymerization by monomer type, active centre or functional groups, by-product, molar-mass control and two examples each.
outline: examples such as PE and PS vs nylon and PET

bank.q: Describe the components of a Ziegler–Natta catalyst and explain how it gives stereochemical control in propene polymerization.
outline: transition metal compound and alkyl aluminium

bank.q: A polymer sample contains equal weights of chains of molar mass 10,000 g mol⁻¹ and 100,000 g mol⁻¹. Calculate Mn, Mw and the polydispersity index. State which average is larger and why.
outline: Mw from weight fractions and M
Mw > Mn because larger chains count more

bank.q: Choose a polymer for a flexible drink bottle and another for a heat-resistant electric iron handle. Justify each choice using chain regularity, branching, cross-linking and crystallinity.
outline: bottle needs toughness and some crystallinity, not high cross-linking
handle needs high softening point, cross-linking or rigid aromatic chains

bank.q: Explain how chemical doping changes polyacetylene from an insulator to a conductor. Name the charge carriers and give the role of oxidation and reduction.
outline: conjugated alternating single and double bonds
p-type doping removes electrons and creates holes

bank.q: For a glass-fibre-reinforced polyester panel, identify the matrix and the reinforcement. Explain the role of a coupling agent, load transfer and the specific modulus advantage.
outline: coupling agent bonds fibre to resin

bank.q: Explain why a polymer sample has no single molar mass. Compare number-average and weight-average molar mass and state which method gives each average.
outline: osmometry gives Mn, light scattering gives Mw, GPC gives distribution

bank.q: Analyse how branching, cross-linking and crystallinity affect density, stiffness, softening point and solubility of a polymer. Use one example for each effect.
outline: cross-linking raises stiffness and stops flow
crystallinity raises density and softening point
solubility falls with cross-linking and crystallinity
examples such as LDPE vs HDPE and vulcanised rubber

bank.q: Evaluate Ziegler–Natta polymerization against free-radical polymerization for making isotactic polypropene. Consider stereocontrol, chain defects, catalyst residues and process conditions.
outline: ZN gives stereocontrol via coordination insertion
radical gives atactic or uncontrolled branching

bank.q: Compare addition and condensation polymers in a table covering monomer, repeat unit, by-product, molar-mass control and recyclability. Assess one advantage and one limitation of each class.
outline: PE and PS vs nylon and PET examples
step growth gives high conversion late
recycling issues for thermosets and composites

bank.q: Design a flexible conducting-polymer sensor and a polymer-matrix composite panel. Justify material choices from conjugation, doping, matrix, reinforcement and interface.
outline: conjugated polymer and dopant for sensor

glossary.def: Chain-growth polymerization in which monomers add to an active centre without losing a small molecule.
A polymer chain in which side groups are arranged randomly along the backbone.
A material made of a matrix and a reinforcement that remain distinct and act together.
Step-growth polymerization between bifunctional monomers, often with loss of a small molecule.
A polymer with a conjugated backbone that conducts after doping.
A polymer built from two or more different monomer types.
Molecule that improves adhesion between matrix and reinforcement in a composite.
Covalent joining of polymer chains into a network that cannot flow.
Ordered packing of polymer chains into regions with a melting point.
Number of repeat units in a polymer chain.
Chemical oxidation or reduction that creates charge carriers in a conducting polymer.
Polymer that stretches and returns to shape because of a loose cross-linked network.
Polymer with all side groups on the same side of the backbone.
Continuous phase in a composite that holds the reinforcement and transfers load.
Small molecule that repeats to form a polymer.
Average molar mass found by dividing total mass by total number of chains.
Ratio Mw/Mn that measures the spread of chain lengths.
Large molecule made of many monomer units joined by covalent bonds.
Strong phase in a composite that carries most of the load.
Modulus divided by density, used to compare stiffness per unit mass.
Polymer with side groups alternating regularly from one side to the other.
Regularity of side-group placement along a chain of stereocentres.
Polymer that softens on heating and can be reshaped because chains are not cross-linked.
Polymer that sets into a network and does not soften on reheating.
Cross-linking of rubber with sulfur to raise strength and elasticity.
Average molar mass in which larger chains contribute more.
